title: Prevention of Chemical Intoxications
path: Toxicology of Drugs and Chemical Substances

headings.title: Public Health Impact and Common Routes of Chemical Exposure
headings.content:
Chemical intoxications remain a major public health concern across Nigeria, affecting both industrial workers and rural households. Exposure occurs when toxic substances enter the human body, leading to acute or chronic poisoning. Understanding how these agents cross physiological barriers determines the severity of the systemic insult.

- **Inhalation**: Breathing in toxic gases, fumes, or dusts, which quickly enter the alveoli and bloodstream.
- **Ingestion**: Swallowing hazardous substances, commonly seen in accidental household poisonings among children or occupational splashes.
- **Dermal absorption**: Direct skin contact with corrosive or lipid-soluble chemicals that penetrate the epidermal barrier.
- **Injection**: Accidental parenteral entry through contaminated needles or high-pressure industrial equipment.

headings.title: Hazardous Chemicals in Nigerian Domestic and Occupational Settings
headings.content: Toxic agents are widely distributed in homes, farms, and factories. Agricultural environments frequently utilize organophosphate pesticides and herbicides, which pose high risks if handlers lack protective gear. In domestic spaces, unlabelled local gin, kerosene, caustic soda used for soap making, and strong bleaching agents are leading causes of accidental poisonings. Industrial settings introduce heavy metals like lead, as well as organic solvents such as benzene and toluene. Recognizing these substances is the first step toward effective mitigation and clinical intervention.

headings.title: Primary Prevention and Safe Storage Practices
headings.content: Primary prevention stops chemical exposure before it happens. Proper physical infrastructure is vital for both factories and homes. Chemicals must never be stored near food items or in beverage containers. Storage facilities require adequate ventilation, temperature control, and secure locks to prevent unauthorized access by children. Every container must feature clear, legible warning labels detailing the specific hazards and basic safety precautions associated with the contents.

headings.title: Role of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) in Risk Reduction
headings.content: When engineering controls fail to eliminate hazards entirely, personal protective equipment serves as the final barrier between the worker and the toxic agent. The choice of PPE depends strictly on the route of exposure. Respiratory masks guard against toxic dusts and vapors, heavy-duty gloves protect against corrosive liquids, and face shields prevent ocular splashes. Nurses must educate workers not only on how to wear PPE correctly, but also on proper inspection, cleaning, and disposal procedures to avoid secondary contamination.

headings.title: Emergency Response, Decontamination, and Antidote Administration
headings.content: Immediate action dictates survival when a chemical poisoning occurs. Decontamination must begin instantly by removing contaminated clothing and flushing affected skin or eyes with copious amounts of clean water for at least fifteen minutes. Healthcare providers must identify the toxin quickly to determine if a specific antidote exists, such as atropine for organophosphate poisoning. Emergency carts must maintain functional suction, airway management tools, and baseline resuscitation drugs.

headings.title: Regulatory Frameworks and Toxicology Surveillance in Nursing
headings.content: Protecting public health requires robust legal enforcement and active nursing surveillance. Regulatory bodies like the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) set safety standards for chemical importation, distribution, and labeling in Nigeria. Community health nurses play a vital role in identifying cluster poisonings, reporting occupational hazards to local health authorities, and educating vulnerable populations on safe chemical management. Surveillance data helps policymakers implement stricter controls on hazardous household and industrial substances.
